doc.title: Iola Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, CT, July 17, 2011

title: The Brubeck Institute and its fellows
summary: The ten-year-old Institute gives young players a protected environment of mentoring, led by Joe Gilman.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Part of paying dues I guess. And the Institute, which is ten years old now?

Yes. And I’m so pleased with what it has done. It has really given these young people who have been fellows there really a start that we just wish that all students that are really talented could have. Because it gives them, right out of high school, one or two years in a protected environment where they just concentrate on being good musicians. And in the process of doing that there are a lot of performances. And in these performances some of them are outreaches where they go into the schools and capture the imagination of younger people thinking well here are these kids and not too much older than they are, wow. They can do that, maybe I can do that. So it generates an interest. And I mean they’ve done well, the kids that have come out of there. Most of them have gone to Juilliard or Manhattan School of Music or the New School. And every once in a while when we’re on the road we run into one of them, saying well, “I’m on my way to Australia,” or, “I’m on my way to Japan,” and it makes you feel really good.

One of them was from near us, from Syracuse I believe, Nick Frenay I think his name was, a trumpet player. That’s really neat, because it’s like almost the way young jazz musicians learned to operate in the world. They would be playing at a young age with mentors.
That’s right. And it’s the opportunity that isn’t given to them so much now. So the thinking behind it was just exactly what you’re saying, that when Dave was coming up

you just played and you hung out with other musicians, you learned from each other, and that opportunity isn’t there now. There aren’t the venues and the opportunity to do that. And the old way had its hazards also, and that’s why — from booze to dope to whatever, and that’s why as I said it’s a protected environment. You have the artistic director, Joe Gilman is for the kids, the executive director, there’s always somebody there. And if somebody breaks any of the rules they’re out and out fast.

Yeah. And when you speak to some of the kids who have gone through that program, one of the answers that I heard that I really like, was he said, “You know I didn’t feel like I was in a jazz studies program. I felt that I was being my own person was being addressed and developed.” And he said, “We learned from each other and we learned how to be a leader” because they rotate on who is going to be the leader of the group. We learned how to compromise, we learned how to respect people with different approaches to music, and by having this little micro cosmos of five kids, all very talented who respect each other, they learn a lot. It’s a crucible for a year or two.
